uslaw-usc-t1-s112a:
Section 112a of Title 1 of the United States Code deals with a treaty book series. The Secretary of State must have the series made and kept up. Its full title is United States Treaties and Other International Agreements. The run starts as of the 1st of January 1950.

The series holds all treaties to which the nation is a party. They are the ones proclaimed in each calendar year as they pass. It also holds pacts that are not treaties in the strict sense. Those are the ones signed or closed in that same year. The book counts as legal proof of its contents in court. That proof holds in the courts of the nation, the states, and the territories.
uslaw-usc-t2-s132a: Section 132a of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with funds for the growth of the general library. It sits in Chapter 5, on the Library of Congress. The left sums of any funds granted by Congress for that end are the subject. Sums that may be granted to the same end in the time to come are in view as well. All such sums are to be laid out as the Joint Committee of Congress on the Library directs.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1402a:
Section 1402a of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with a first look at claims. It sits in Chapter 24, on the duties of Congress to its staff, in a part on ways to settle rows. A claim sent to the office that hires the man is the start point. No more than seven days past that send, the Executive Director is to name a hearing officer. That officer is to make a first look at the claim.

The way that officer is named is set by the text. The name is to be made in the same way, and by the same rules and steps, as the naming of such an officer under a named part of Section 1405. A second clause deals with the points that must be weighed at that first look.
uslaw-usc-t2-s142a: Section 142a of Title 2 of the United States Code abolishes an office in the Library of Congress. From June 10, 1928 onward, the office of administrative assistant and disbursing officer of the Library, created by section 142 of the same title, no longer exists. The duties that the office once performed are instead carried out, under the direction of the Librarian of Congress, by people the Librarian appoints for those purposes.
uslaw-usc-t2-s162a:
Section 162a of Title 2 of the United States Code caps the gross salary of Library of Congress staff who also receive outside honoraria. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on the Library of Congress. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. It works with a linked section on such payments.

Hereafter, the gross salary of any Library post that is topped up by an honorarium from non appropriated funds is capped, the text states. Salary plus honorarium together may not pass the maximum salary set for the grade. The rule stops outside payments from lifting a federal salary past its lawful ceiling.
uslaw-usc-t2-s182a:
Section 182a of Title 2 of the United States Code sets up a revolving fund for duplication services. It sits in Chapter 5 of that title, on the Library of Congress. Part (a) creates the fund in the Treasury. The fund serves the duplication and delivery services of the Librarian of Congress. Those services are tied to the national audiovisual conservation center.

That center was set up under an act on the purchase of land for the Library of Congress. The name Librarian, in sections 182a to 182d, means the Librarian of Congress. The section goes on to state the terms of the fund. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1862a:
Section 1862a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the use of building project funds to repay the Capitol Police. It sits in Chapter 28 of that title, on the Architect of the Capitol, in the part on appropriations and spending. Part (a) deals with the pay of overtime costs. The Architect of the Capitol is to move sums to the Capitol Police accounts.

The sums are those made open for building projects in a fiscal year. They go to the right appropriation accounts of the United States Capitol Police. The end is to repay the Capitol Police for overtime costs run up in connection with such projects. Part (b) of the section states its date of effect. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2162a:
Section 2162a of Title 2 of the United States Code orders the thriftiest running of the Capitol Power Plant. The Architect of the Capitol must take the steps needed to run the plant's steam boilers in the most energy-wise way. The aim is to cut carbon output and running costs. Steps named include changing steam pressures and matching boiler work to shifts in demand, including the seasons. The boiler steps were due within thirty days after 19 December 2007.

The same duty covers the plant's cooling side. The Architect must run the chiller plant in the most energy-wise way, again to cut carbon output and costs. Steps named include changing water temperatures and matching chiller work to demand and season.
uslaw-usc-t2-s282a:
Section 282a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers staff of the Office of Legislative Counsel in the House. It sits in Chapter 9 of that title, on that office, in the House part on administration. Part (a) states how staff are hired. With the approval of the Speaker, the Legislative Counsel is to appoint such lawyers and other staff as may be needed. The Speaker may act through rules and paths he has approved instead.

The staff must be such as are needed for the swift and sound work of the office. A bar on bias is stated for such hiring. Each appointment is to be made without regard to the politics of the person hired, as the text goes on to state. The heading also covers a Deputy Legislative Counsel and the handing on of tasks.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2a:
Section 2a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers reapportionment of Representatives among the states after each census. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on election of senators and representatives. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. House seats shift with population every ten years.

On the first day, or within one week after, of set sessions of Congress, the President must act, the text states. The President transmits a statement to Congress based on the decennial census figures. That statement gives the number of representatives each state is entitled to. The Clerk of the House then has duties to notify the states. Census numbers thus become seat numbers by a fixed chain.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5322a:
Section 5322a of Title 2 of the United States Code creates an allowance to pay interns in member offices. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on House members and their employees. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. It is the member office twin of a leadership office rule.

An allowance is established for the House for the pay of interns who serve in member offices. A cap on the amount available is set in the next part of the section. That cap limits how much any office can draw for intern pay. The rule funds early career help in the offices where constituents are served day to day.
